[{"name":"Albert Einstein","identifier":736,"abstract":"Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the theory of relativity. Einstein also made important contributions to quantum theory. His mass–energy equivalence formula E = mc⁲, which arises from special relativity, has been called \"the world's most famous equation\". He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for \"his services to theoretical physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect\". Born as a subject to the Kingdom of Württemberg, part of the German Empire which he later renounced on 28 January 1896, just 6 weeks before he turned 17, avoiding conscription into military service. In 1895, he moved to Pavia to stay with his family which moved there an year earlier and then to Swiss canton of Aarau, to attend an year of cantonal school. In 1896, at the age of seventeen, he enrolled in the mathematics and physics teaching diploma program at the Swiss federal polytechnic school in Zurich, graduating in 1900. He acquired Swiss citizenship a year later, which he kept for the rest of his life, and afterwards secured a permanent position at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern. In 1905, he submitted a successful PhD dissertation to the University of Zurich. In 1914, he moved to Berlin to join the Prussian Academy of Sciences and the Humboldt University of Berlin, becoming director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics in 1917; he also became a Prussian and consequently also German citizen again. In 1933, while Einstein was visiting the United States, Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany. Horrified by the Nazi persecution of his fellow Jews, he decided to remain in the US, and was granted American citizenship in 1940. On the eve of World War II, he endorsed a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt alerting him to the potential German nuclear weapons program and recommending that the US begin similar research, later carried out as the Manhattan Project. In 1905, sometimes described as his annus mirabilis, he published four groundbreaking papers. In them, he outlined a theory of the photoelectric effect, explained Brownian motion, introduced his special theory of relativity, and demonstrated that if the special theory is correct, mass and energy are equivalent to each other. In 1915, he proposed a general theory of relativity that extended his system of mechanics to incorporate gravitation. A paper that he published the following year laid out the implications of general relativity for the modeling of the structure and evolution of the universe as a whole. It introduced the cosmological constant and is further regarded as the first step in the field of modern theoretical cosmology. In 1917, Einstein wrote a paper which introduced the concepts of spontaneous emission and stimulated emission, the latter of which is the core mechanism behind the laser and maser, and which contained a trove of information that would be beneficial to developments in physics later on, such as quantum electrodynamics and quantum optics. In the middle part of his career, Einstein made important contributions to statistical mechanics and quantum theory. Especially notable was his work on the quantum physics of radiation, in which light consists of particles, subsequently called photons. With physicist Satyendra Nath Bose, he laid the groundwork for Bose–Einstein statistics. For much of the last phase of his academic life, Einstein worked on two endeavors that ultimately proved unsuccessful. First, he advocated against quantum theory's introduction of fundamental randomness into science's picture of the world, objecting that \"God does not play dice\". Second, he attempted to devise a unified field theory by generalizing his geometric theory of gravitation to include electromagnetism. As a result, he became increasingly isolated from mainstream modern physics. Many things are named after him, including the element Einsteinium. In 1999, he was named Time's Person of the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Conscription_in_Germany\" title=\"Conscription in Germany\" id=\"mwWA\"\u003econscription into military service\u003c/a\u003e.\u003csup about=\"#mwt85\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-10\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" In 1896, at the age of seventeen, he enrolled in the mathematics and physics teaching diploma program at the Swiss \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./ETH_Zurich\" title=\"ETH Zurich\" id=\"mwYQ\"\u003efederal polytechnic school\u003c/a\u003e in Zurich, graduating in 1900. He acquired Swiss citizenship a year later, which he kept for the rest of his life, and afterwards secured a permanent position at the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Swiss_Patent_Office\" title=\"Swiss Patent Office\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwYg\"\u003eSwiss Patent Office\u003c/a\u003e in \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Bern\" title=\"Bern\" id=\"mwYw\"\u003eBern\u003c/a\u003e. In 1905, he submitted a successful \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./PhD\" title=\"PhD\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwZA\"\u003ePhD\u003c/a\u003e dissertation to the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./University_of_Zurich\" title=\"University of Zurich\" id=\"mwZQ\"\u003eUniversity of Zurich\u003c/a\u003e. In 1914, he moved to Berlin to join the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Prussian_Academy_of_Sciences\" title=\"Prussian Academy of Sciences\" id=\"mwZg\"\u003ePrussian Academy of Sciences\u003c/a\u003e and the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Humboldt_University_of_Berlin\" title=\"Humboldt University of Berlin\" id=\"mwZw\"\u003eHumboldt University of Berlin\u003c/a\u003e, becoming director of the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Kaiser_Wilhelm_Institute_for_Physics\" title=\"Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwaA\"\u003eKaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics\u003c/a\u003e in 1917; he also became a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Prussia\" title=\"Prussia\" id=\"mwaQ\"\u003ePrussian\u003c/a\u003e and consequently also German citizen again. In 1933, while Einstein was visiting the United States, \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Adolf_Hitler's_rise_to_power\" title=\"Adolf Hitler's rise to power\" id=\"mwag\"\u003eAdolf Hitler came to power\u003c/a\u003e in Germany. Horrified by the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Nazi_Germany\" title=\"Nazi Germany\" id=\"mwaw\"\u003eNazi\u003c/a\u003e persecution of his fellow Jews,\u003csup about=\"#mwt86\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-zE9Bz_11-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"zE9Bz\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-zE9Bz-11\" id=\"mwbA\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwbQ\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwbg\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e9\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwbw\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e he decided to remain in the US, and was granted American citizenship in 1940.\u003csup about=\"#mwt87\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-BoyerDubofsky2001_12-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"BoyerDubofsky2001\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-BoyerDubofsky2001-12\" id=\"mwcA\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwcQ\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwcg\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e10\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwcw\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e On the eve of \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./World_War_II\" title=\"World War II\" id=\"mwdA\"\u003eWorld War II\u003c/a\u003e, he endorsed \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Einstein–Szilard_letter\" title=\"Einstein–Szilard letter\" id=\"mwdQ\"\u003ea letter\u003c/a\u003e to President \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Franklin_D._Roosevelt\" title=\"Franklin D. Roosevelt\" id=\"mwdg\"\u003eFranklin D. Roosevelt\u003c/a\u003e alerting him to the potential \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./German_nuclear_weapons_program\" title=\"German nuclear weapons program\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwdw\"\u003eGerman nuclear weapons program\u003c/a\u003e and recommending that the US begin similar research, later carried out as the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Manhattan_Project\" title=\"Manhattan Project\" id=\"mweA\"\u003eManhattan Project\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mweQ\"\u003eIn 1905, sometimes described as his \u003ci id=\"mweg\"\u003e\u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Annus_mirabilis\" title=\"Annus mirabilis\" id=\"mwew\"\u003eannus mirabilis\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/i\u003e (miracle year), he published \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Annus_mirabilis_papers\" title=\"Annus mirabilis papers\" id=\"mwfA\"\u003efour groundbreaking papers\u003c/a\u003e.\u003csup about=\"#mwt88\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGalison2000377_13-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"group\":\"\",\"name\":\"FOOTNOTEGalison2000377\"},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalison2000377-13\"},\"parts\":[{\"template\":{\"target\":{\"wt\":\"sfnp\",\"href\":\"./Template:Sfnp\"},\"params\":{\"1\":{\"wt\":\"Galison\"},\"2\":{\"wt\":\"2000\"},\"p\":{\"wt\":\"377\"}},\"i\":0}}]}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalison2000377-13\" id=\"mwfQ\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwfg\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwfw\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e11\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwgA\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e In them, he outlined a theory of the photoelectric effect, explained \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Brownian_motion\" title=\"Brownian motion\" id=\"mwgQ\"\u003eBrownian motion\u003c/a\u003e, introduced his special theory of relativity, and demonstrated that if the special theory is correct, mass and energy are equivalent to each other. In 1915, he proposed a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./General_theory_of_relativity\" title=\"General theory of relativity\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwgg\"\u003egeneral theory of relativity\u003c/a\u003e that extended his system of mechanics to incorporate \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Gravitation\" title=\"Gravitation\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwgw\"\u003egravitation\u003c/a\u003e. A paper that he published the following year laid out the implications of general relativity for the modeling of the structure and evolution of the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Universe\" title=\"Universe\" id=\"mwhA\"\u003euniverse\u003c/a\u003e as a whole.\u003csup about=\"#mwt91\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-Nobel_14-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"Nobel\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-Nobel-14\" id=\"mwhQ\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwhg\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwhw\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e12\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwiA\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003csup about=\"#mwt92\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-NYT-20151124_15-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"NYT-20151124\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-NYT-20151124-15\" id=\"mwiQ\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwig\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwiw\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e13\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwjA\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e It introduced the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Cosmological_constant\" title=\"Cosmological constant\" id=\"mwjQ\"\u003ecosmological constant\u003c/a\u003e and is further regarded as the first step in the field of modern theoretical \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Cosmology\" title=\"Cosmology\" id=\"mwjg\"\u003ecosmology\u003c/a\u003e. In 1917, Einstein wrote a paper which introduced the concepts of \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Spontaneous_emission\" title=\"Spontaneous emission\" id=\"mwjw\"\u003espontaneous emission\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Stimulated_emission\" title=\"Stimulated emission\" id=\"mwkA\"\u003estimulated emission\u003c/a\u003e, the latter of which is the core mechanism behind the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Laser\" title=\"Laser\" id=\"mwkQ\"\u003elaser\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Maser\" title=\"Maser\" id=\"mwkg\"\u003emaser\u003c/a\u003e, and which contained a trove of information that would be beneficial to developments in physics later on, such as \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Quantum_electrodynamics\" title=\"Quantum electrodynamics\" id=\"mwkw\"\u003equantum electrodynamics\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Quantum_optics\" title=\"Quantum optics\" id=\"mwlA\"\u003equantum optics\u003c/a\u003e.\u003csup about=\"#mwt95\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-16\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-16\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-16\" id=\"mwlQ\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwlg\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwlw\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e14\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwmA\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwmQ\"\u003eIn the middle part of his career, Einstein made important contributions to \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Statistical_mechanics\" title=\"Statistical mechanics\" id=\"mwmg\"\u003estatistical mechanics\u003c/a\u003e and quantum theory. Especially notable was his work on the quantum physics of \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Radiation\" title=\"Radiation\" id=\"mwmw\"\u003eradiation\u003c/a\u003e, in which light consists of particles, subsequently called \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Photon\" title=\"Photon\" id=\"mwnA\"\u003ephotons\u003c/a\u003e. With physicist \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Satyendra_Nath_Bose\" title=\"Satyendra Nath Bose\" id=\"mwnQ\"\u003eSatyendra Nath Bose\u003c/a\u003e, he laid the groundwork for \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Bose–Einstein_statistics\" title=\"Bose–Einstein statistics\" id=\"mwng\"\u003eBose–Einstein statistics\u003c/a\u003e. For much of the last phase of his academic life, Einstein worked on two endeavors that ultimately proved unsuccessful. First, he advocated against quantum theory's introduction of fundamental randomness into science's picture of the world, objecting that \"God does not play dice\".\u003csup about=\"#mwt98\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-17\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-17\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-17\" id=\"mwnw\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwoA\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwoQ\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e15\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwog\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Second, he attempted to devise a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Unified_field_theory\" title=\"Unified field theory\" id=\"mwow\"\u003eunified field theory\u003c/a\u003e by generalizing his geometric theory of gravitation to include \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Electromagnetism\" title=\"Electromagnetism\" id=\"mwpA\"\u003eelectromagnetism\u003c/a\u003e. As a result, he became increasingly isolated from mainstream \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Modern_physics\" title=\"Modern physics\" id=\"mwpQ\"\u003emodern physics\u003c/a\u003e. Many \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./List_of_things_named_after_Albert_Einstein\" title=\"List of things named after Albert Einstein\" id=\"mwpg\"\u003ethings are named after him\u003c/a\u003e, including the element \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Einsteinium\" title=\"Einsteinium\" id=\"mwpw\"\u003eEinsteinium\u003c/a\u003e. Bose\u003c/a\u003e derived the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Planck_spectrum\" title=\"Planck spectrum\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwAwM\"\u003ePlanck spectrum\u003c/a\u003e in 1924. In 1911, he first calculated the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Gravitational_lens\" title=\"Gravitational lens\" id=\"mwAyw\"\u003egravitational deflection of light\u003c/a\u003e passing close to the Sun, a prediction later adjusted upon completion of the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./General_relativity\" title=\"General relativity\" id=\"mwAy0\"\u003egeneral theory of relativity\u003c/a\u003e. He reworked his calculation in 1913, having now found a way to model gravitation with the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Riemann_curvature_tensor\" title=\"Riemann curvature tensor\" id=\"mwAy4\"\u003eRiemann curvature tensor\u003c/a\u003e of a non-Euclidean four-dimensional \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Spacetime\" title=\"Spacetime\" id=\"mwAy8\"\u003espacetime\u003c/a\u003e. By the fall of 1915, his reimagining of the mathematics of gravitation in terms of Riemannian geometry was complete, and he applied his new theory not just to the behavior of the Sun as a gravitational lens but also to another astronomical phenomenon, the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Precession_of_the_perihelion_of_Mercury\" title=\"Precession of the perihelion of Mercury\" attitude to life ... He devoted six months to a tour of Asia that saw him speaking in Japan, Singapore and Sri Lanka (then known as \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Ceylon\" title=\"Ceylon\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwA2s\"\u003eCeylon\u003c/a\u003e). After his first public lecture in Tokyo, he met \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Emperor_Yoshihito\" title=\"Emperor Yoshihito\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwA2w\"\u003eEmperor Yoshihito\u003c/a\u003e and his wife at the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Tokyo_Imperial_Palace\" title=\"Tokyo Imperial Palace\" id=\"mwA20\"\u003eImperial Palace\u003c/a\u003e, with thousands of spectators thronging the streets in the hope of catching a glimpse of him. (In a letter to his sons, he wrote that Japanese people seemed to him to be generally modest, intelligent and considerate, and to have a true appreciation of art.\u003csup about=\"#mwt369\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-FOOTNOTEIsaacson2007307–308_113-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"group\":\"\",\"name\":\"FOOTNOTEIsaacson2007307–308\"},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEIsaacson2007307–308-113\"},\"parts\":[{\"template\":{\"target\":{\"wt\":\"sfnp\",\"href\":\"./Template:Sfnp\"},\"params\":{\"1\":{\"wt\":\"Isaacson\"},\"2\":{\"wt\":\"2007\"},\"p\":{\"wt\":\"307–308\"}},\"i\":0}}]}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIsaacson2007307–308-113\" id=\"mwA24\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwA28\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwA3A\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e107\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwA3E\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e But his picture of them in his diary was less flattering: \"[the] intellectual needs of this nation seem to be weaker than their artistic ones – natural disposition?\" His journal also contains views of China and India which were uncomplimentary. Of Chinese people, he wrote that \"even the children are spiritless and look obtuse... It would be a pity if these Chinese supplant all other races. For the likes of us the mere thought is unspeakably dreary\".\u003csup about=\"#mwt375\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-38YkY_114-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"38YkY\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-38YkY-114\" id=\"mwA3I\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwA3M\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwA3Q\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e108\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwA3U\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003csup about=\"#mwt378\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-115\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-115\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-115\" id=\"mwA3Y\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwA3c\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwA3g\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e109\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwA3k\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e) He was greeted with even greater enthusiasm on the last leg of his tour, in which he spent twelve days in \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Mandatory_Palestine\" title=\"Mandatory Palestine\" id=\"mwA3o\"\u003eMandatory Palestine\u003c/a\u003e, newly entrusted to British rule by the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./League_of_Nations\" title=\"League of Nations\" id=\"mwA3s\"\u003eLeague of Nations\u003c/a\u003e in the aftermath of the First World War. \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Sir_Herbert_Samuel\" title=\"Sir Herbert Samuel\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwA3w\"\u003eSir Herbert Samuel\u003c/a\u003e, the British High Commissioner, welcomed him with a degree of ceremony normally only accorded to a visiting head of state, including a cannon salute. Caltech supported him in his wish that he should not be exposed to quite as much attention from the media as he had experienced when visiting the US in 1921, and he therefore declined all the invitations to receive prizes or make speeches that his admirers poured down upon him. In February and March 1933, the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Gestapo\" title=\"Gestapo\" id=\"mwBDA\"\u003eGestapo\u003c/a\u003e repeatedly raided his family's apartment in Berlin.\u003csup about=\"#mwt441\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-134\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-134\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-134\" id=\"mwBDE\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwBDI\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBDM\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e128\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBDQ\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e He and his wife Elsa returned to Europe in March, and during the trip, they learned that the German Reichstag had passed the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Enabling_Act_of_1933\" title=\"Enabling Act of 1933\" id=\"mwBDU\"\u003eEnabling Act\u003c/a\u003e on 23 March, transforming Hitler's government into a \u003ci id=\"mwBDY\"\u003ede facto\u003c/i\u003e legal dictatorship, and that they would not be able to proceed to Berlin. Later on, they heard that their cottage had been raided by the Nazis and Einstein's personal sailboat confiscated. In his late journals he wrote:\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003clink rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1244412712\" about=\"#mwt678\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/templatestyles mw:Transclusion\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"templatestyles\",\"attrs\":{\"src\":\"Template:Blockquote/styles.css\"},\"parts\":[{\"template\":{\"target\":{\"wt\":\"blockquote\",\"href\":\"./Template:Blockquote\"},\"params\":{\"1\":{\"wt\":\"If I were not a physicist, I would probably be a musician. I often think in music. I live my daydreams in music. I see my life in terms of music\u003cspan class=\"nowrap\"\u003e\u003cspan typeof=\"mw:Entity\"\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e... I get most joy in life out of music.\u003csup about=\"#mwt680\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-BQH5A_218-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"BQH5A\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-BQH5A-218\" id=\"mwBtQ\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwBtU\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBtY\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e211\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBtc\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003csup about=\"#mwt682\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-aBOjz_219-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"aBOjz\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-aBOjz-219\" id=\"mwBtg\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwBtk\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBto\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e212\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBts\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwBtw\"\u003eHis mother played the piano reasonably well and wanted her son to learn the violin, not only to instill in him a love of music but also to help him assimilate into \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./German_culture\" title=\"German culture\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwBt0\"\u003eGerman culture\u003c/a\u003e. According to conductor \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Leon_Botstein\" title=\"Leon Botstein\" id=\"mwBt4\"\u003eLeon Botstein\u003c/a\u003e, Einstein began playing when he was 5. However, he did not enjoy it at that age.\u003csup about=\"#mwt684\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-Botstein_220-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"Botstein\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-Botstein-220\" id=\"mwBt8\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwBuA\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBuE\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e213\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBuI\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwBuM\"\u003eWhen he turned 13, he discovered \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Mozart\" title=\"Mozart\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwBuQ\"\u003eMozart\u003c/a\u003e's \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Mozart_violin_sonatas\" title=\"Mozart violin sonatas\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwBuU\"\u003eviolin sonatas\u003c/a\u003e, whereupon he became enamored of Mozart's compositions and studied music more willingly. Einstein taught himself to play without \"ever practicing systematically\". He said that \"love is a better teacher than a sense of duty\".\u003csup about=\"#mwt686\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-Botstein_220-1\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"Botstein\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-Botstein-220\" id=\"mwBuY\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwBuc\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBug\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e213\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBuk\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Einstein actively participated in local music sessions, playing the violin alongside Ernestina Marangoni playing the pianoforte in Pavia and \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Casteggio\" title=\"Casteggio\" id=\"mwBuo\"\u003eCasteggio\u003c/a\u003e, a period from 1895 to 1900 when he visited the Marangoni family. At the age of 17, he was heard by a school examiner in Aarau while playing \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Beethoven\" title=\"Beethoven\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwBus\"\u003eBeethoven\u003c/a\u003e's \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Beethoven's_violin_sonatas_(disambiguation)\" title=\"Beethoven's violin sonatas (disambiguation)\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwBuw\"\u003eviolin sonatas\u003c/a\u003e. What struck the examiner, writes Botstein, was that Einstein \"displayed a deep love of the music, a quality that was and remains in short supply. Music possessed an unusual meaning for this student.\"\u003csup about=\"#mwt687\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-Botstein_220-2\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"Botstein\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-Botstein-220\" id=\"mwBu4\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwBu8\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBvA\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e213\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwBvE\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwBvI\"\u003eMusic took on a pivotal and permanent role in Einstein's life from that period on. Although the idea of becoming a professional musician himself was not on his mind at any time, among those with whom Einstein played \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Chamber_music\" title=\"Chamber music\" id=\"mwBvM\"\u003echamber music\u003c/a\u003e were a few professionals, including Kurt Appelbaum, and he performed for private audiences and friends. Chamber music had also become a regular part of his social life while living in Bern, Zurich, and Berlin, where he played with Max Planck and his son, among others. Ordinarily, the density fluctuations are controlled by the second derivative of the free energy with respect to the density. At the critical point, this derivative is zero, leading to large fluctuations. The effect of density fluctuations is that light of all wavelengths is scattered, making the fluid look milky white. Einstein relates this to \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Rayleigh_scattering\" title=\"Rayleigh scattering\" id=\"mwB4o\"\u003eRayleigh scattering\u003c/a\u003e, which is what happens when the fluctuation size is much smaller than the wavelength, and which explains why the sky is blue.\u003csup about=\"#mwt726\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-L2N73_242-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" id=\"mwCDY\"\u003eGeneral relativity\u003c/a\u003e (GR) is a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Theory_of_gravitation\" title=\"Theory of gravitation\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwCDc\"\u003etheory According to it, the observed gravitational attraction between masses results from the warping of \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Spacetime\" title=\"Spacetime\" id=\"mwCDg\"\u003espacetime\u003c/a\u003e by those masses. General relativity has developed into an essential tool in modern \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Astrophysics\" title=\"Astrophysics\" id=\"mwCDk\"\u003eastrophysics\u003c/a\u003e; it provides the foundation for the current understanding of \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Black_holes\" title=\"Black holes\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwCDo\"\u003eblack holes\u003c/a\u003e, regions of id=\"mwCD4\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwCD8\"\u003eAs Einstein later said, the reason for the development of general relativity was that the preference of inertial motions within \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Special_relativity\" title=\"Special relativity\" id=\"mwCEA\"\u003especial relativity\u003c/a\u003e In that article titled \"On the Relativity Principle and the Conclusions Drawn from It\", he argued that \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Free_fall\" title=\"Free fall\" id=\"mwCEU\"\u003efree fall\u003c/a\u003e is really inertial motion, and that for a free-falling observer the rules of special relativity must apply. This argument is called the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Equivalence_principle\" title=\"Equivalence principle\" id=\"mwCEY\"\u003eequivalence principle\u003c/a\u003e. rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Gravitational_lensing\" title=\"Gravitational lensing\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwCEk\"\u003egravitational lensing\u003c/a\u003e.\u003csup about=\"#mwt769\" He gave up looking for fully generally covariant tensor equations and searched for equations that would be invariant under general linear transformations only.\u003csup about=\"#mwt790\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-271\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-271\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-271\" id=\"mwCJI\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCJM\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCJQ\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e262\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCJU\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwCJY\"\u003eIn June 1913, the Entwurf ('draft') theory was the result of these investigations. As its name suggests, it was a sketch of a theory, less elegant and more difficult than general relativity, with the equations of motion supplemented by additional gauge fixing conditions. The energy and momentum derived within general relativity by \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Emmy_Noether\" title=\"Emmy Noether\" id=\"mwCRg\"\u003eNoether\u003c/a\u003e's prescriptions do not make a real tensor for this reason.\u003csup about=\"#mwt825\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-290\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-290\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-290\" id=\"mwCRk\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCRo\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCRs\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e281\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCRw\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwCR0\"\u003eEinstein argued that this is true for a fundamental reason: the gravitational field could be made to vanish by a choice of coordinates. He maintained that the non-covariant energy momentum pseudotensor was, in fact, the best description of the energy momentum distribution in a gravitational field. While the use of non-covariant objects like pseudotensors was criticized by \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Erwin_Schrödinger\" title=\"Erwin Schrödinger\" id=\"mwCR4\"\u003eErwin A curved path like an orbit is not the result of a force deflecting a body from an ideal straight-line path, but rather the body's attempt to fall freely through a background that is itself curved by the presence of other masses. A remark by \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./John_Archibald_Wheeler\" title=\"John Archibald Wheeler\" id=\"mwCUY\"\u003eJohn Archibald Wheeler\u003c/a\u003e that has become proverbial among physicists summarizes the theory: \"Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve.\"\u003csup about=\"#mwt838\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-Wheeler_295-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"name\":\"Wheeler\"},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Wheeler-295\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-Wheeler-295\" id=\"mwCUc\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCUg\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCUk\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e286\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCUo\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003csup about=\"#mwt841\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-296\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-296\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-296\" id=\"mwCUs\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCUw\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCU0\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e287\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCU4\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Einstein_field_equations\" title=\"Einstein field equations\" id=\"mwCU8\"\u003eEinstein field equations\u003c/a\u003e cover the latter aspect of the theory, relating the curvature of spacetime to the distribution of matter and energy. The \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Geodesic_equation\" title=\"Geodesic equation\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwCVA\"\u003egeodesic equation\u003c/a\u003e covers the former aspect, stating that freely falling bodies follow \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Geodesics_in_general_relativity\" title=\"Geodesics in general relativity\" id=\"mwCVE\"\u003elines that are as straight as possible in a curved spacetime\u003c/a\u003e. Einstein regarded this as an \"independent fundamental assumption\" that had to be postulated in addition to the field equations in order to complete the theory. Believing this to be a shortcoming in how general relativity was originally presented, he wished to derive it from the field equations themselves. Since the equations of general relativity are non-linear, a lump of energy made out of pure gravitational fields, like a black hole, would move on a trajectory which is determined by the Einstein field equations themselves, not by a new law. Accordingly, Einstein proposed that the field equations would determine the path of a singular solution, like a black hole, to be a geodesic. Both physicists and philosophers have often repeated the assertion that the geodesic equation can be obtained from applying the field equations to the motion of a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" solid\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwCYA\"\u003eIn 1907, Einstein proposed a model of matter where each atom in a lattice structure is an independent harmonic oscillator. In the Einstein model, each atom oscillates independently—a series of equally spaced quantized states for each oscillator. Einstein was aware that getting the frequency of the actual oscillations would be difficult, but he nevertheless proposed this theory because it was a particularly clear demonstration that quantum mechanics could solve the specific heat problem in classical mechanics. \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Peter_Debye\" title=\"Peter Debye\" id=\"mwCYE\"\u003ePeter Debye\u003c/a\u003e refined this model.\u003csup about=\"#mwt857\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-ixm32_300-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" Soon, this idea attracted the attention of Einstein and his assistant \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Otto_Stern\" title=\"Otto Stern\" id=\"mwCbk\"\u003eOtto Stern\u003c/a\u003e. However, after publishing the findings, they promptly withdrew their support, because they no longer had confidence in the correctness of the idea of zero-point energy.\u003csup about=\"#mwt866\" id=\"mwCfc\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCfg\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCfk\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e303\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCfs\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCfw\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCf0\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e304\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCf4\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Their debates would influence later \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Interpretations_of_quantum_mechanics\" id=\"mwCgA\"\u003e\u003ch4 data-mw-wikitext=\"\" id=\"Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen_paradox\"\u003e\u003cspan id=\"Einstein.E2.80.93Podolsky.E2.80.93Rosen_paradox\" typeof=\"mw:FallbackId\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003eEinstein–Podolsky–Rosen paradox\u003c/h4\u003e\n\u003cspan class=\"mw-empty-elt\" about=\"#mwt886\" typeof=\"mw:Transclusion\" data-mw='{\"parts\":[{\"template\":{\"target\":{\"wt\":\"Main\",\"href\":\"./Template:Main\"},\"params\":{\"1\":{\"wt\":\"EPR paradox\"}},\"i\":0}}]}' id=\"mwCgE\"\u003e\u003clink rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" about=\"#mwt887\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/templatestyles\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"templatestyles\",\"attrs\":{\"src\":\"Module:Hatnote/styles.css\"},\"body\":{\"extsrc\":\"\"}}'/\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\" about=\"#mwt886\" id=\"mwCgI\"\u003eMain article: \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./EPR_paradox\" title=\"EPR paradox\" class=\"mw-redirect\"\u003eEPR paradox\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwCgM\"\u003eEinstein never fully accepted quantum mechanics. While he recognized that it made correct predictions, he believed a more fundamental description of nature must be possible. Over the years he presented multiple arguments to this effect, but the one he preferred most dated to a debate with Bohr in 1930. Einstein suggested a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Einstein's_thought_experiments\" title=\"Einstein's thought experiments\" id=\"mwCgQ\"\u003ethought experiment\u003c/a\u003e in which two objects are allowed to interact and then moved apart a great distance from each other. The quantum-mechanical description of the two objects is a mathematical entity known as a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Wavefunction\" title=\"Wavefunction\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwCgU\"\u003ewavefunction\u003c/a\u003e. If the wavefunction that describes the two objects before their interaction is given, then the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Schrödinger_equation\" title=\"Schrödinger equation\" id=\"mwCgY\"\u003eSchrödinger equation\u003c/a\u003e provides the wavefunction that describes them after their interaction. But because of what would later be called \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Quantum_entanglement\" title=\"Quantum entanglement\" id=\"mwCgc\"\u003equantum entanglement\u003c/a\u003e, measuring one object would lead to an instantaneous change of the wavefunction describing the other object, no matter how far away it is. Moreover, the choice of which measurement to perform upon the first object would affect what wavefunction could result for the second object. Einstein reasoned that no influence could propagate from the first object to the second instantaneously fast. Indeed, he argued, physics depends on being able to tell one thing apart from another, and such instantaneous influences would call that into question. Because the true \"physical condition\" of the second object could not be immediately altered by an action done to the first, Einstein concluded, the wavefunction could not be that true physical condition, only an incomplete description of it.\u003csup about=\"#mwt888\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHoward1990_314-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"group\":\"\",\"name\":\"FOOTNOTEHoward1990\"},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoward1990-314\"},\"parts\":[{\"template\":{\"target\":{\"wt\":\"sfnp\",\"href\":\"./Template:Sfnp\"},\"params\":{\"1\":{\"wt\":\"Howard\"},\"2\":{\"wt\":\"1990\"}},\"i\":0}}]}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoward1990-314\" id=\"mwCgg\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCgk\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCgo\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e305\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCgs\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003csup about=\"#mwt891\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHarriganSpekkens2010_315-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"group\":\"\",\"name\":\"FOOTNOTEHarriganSpekkens2010\"},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriganSpekkens2010-315\"},\"parts\":[{\"template\":{\"target\":{\"wt\":\"sfnp\",\"href\":\"./Template:Sfnp\"},\"params\":{\"1\":{\"wt\":\"Harrigan\"},\"2\":{\"wt\":\"Spekkens\"},\"3\":{\"wt\":\"2010\"}},\"i\":0}}]}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriganSpekkens2010-315\" id=\"mwCgw\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCg0\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCg4\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e306\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCg8\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwChA\"\u003eA more famous version of this argument came in 1935, when Einstein published a paper with \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Boris_Podolsky\" title=\"Boris Podolsky\" id=\"mwChE\"\u003eBoris Podolsky\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Nathan_Rosen\" title=\"Nathan Rosen\" id=\"mwChI\"\u003eNathan Rosen\u003c/a\u003e that laid out what would become known as the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./EPR_paradox\" title=\"EPR paradox\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwChM\"\u003eEPR paradox\u003c/a\u003e.\u003csup about=\"#mwt897\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-316\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-316\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-316\" id=\"mwChQ\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwChU\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwChY\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e307\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwChc\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e In this thought experiment, two particles interact in such a way that the wavefunction describing them is entangled. Then, no matter how far the two particles were separated, a precise position measurement on one particle would imply the ability to predict, perfectly, the result of measuring the position of the other particle. Likewise, a precise momentum measurement of one particle would result in an equally precise prediction for the momentum of the other particle, without needing to disturb the other particle in any way. They argued that no action taken on the first particle could instantaneously affect the other, since this would involve information being transmitted faster than light, which is forbidden by the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Theory_of_relativity\" title=\"Theory of relativity\" id=\"mwChg\"\u003etheory of relativity\u003c/a\u003e. They invoked a principle, later known as the \"EPR criterion of reality\", positing that: \"If, without in any way disturbing a system, we can predict with certainty (i.e., with \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Probability\" title=\"Probability\" id=\"mwChk\"\u003eprobability\u003c/a\u003e equal to unity) the value of a physical quantity, then there exists an element of reality corresponding to that quantity.\" From this, they inferred that the second particle must have a definite value of both position and of momentum prior to either quantity being measured. But quantum mechanics considers these two observables \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Observable#Incompatibility_of_observables_in_quantum_mechanics\" title=\"Observable\" id=\"mwCho\"\u003eincompatible\u003c/a\u003e and thus does not associate simultaneous values for both to any system. Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen therefore concluded that quantum theory does not provide a complete description of reality.\u003csup about=\"#mwt894\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPeres2002_317-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{\"group\":\"\",\"name\":\"FOOTNOTEPeres2002\"},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeres2002-317\"},\"parts\":[{\"template\":{\"target\":{\"wt\":\"sfnp\",\"href\":\"./Template:Sfnp\"},\"params\":{\"1\":{\"wt\":\"Peres\"},\"2\":{\"wt\":\"2002\"}},\"i\":0}}]}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeres2002-317\" id=\"mwChs\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwChw\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCh0\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e308\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCh4\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwCh8\"\u003eIn 1964, \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./John_Stewart_Bell\" title=\"John Stewart Bell\" id=\"mwCiA\"\u003eJohn Stewart Bell\u003c/a\u003e carried the analysis of quantum entanglement much further. He deduced that if measurements are performed independently on the two separated particles of an entangled pair, then the assumption that the outcomes depend upon hidden variables within each half implies a mathematical constraint on how the outcomes on the two measurements are correlated. This constraint would later be called a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Bell_inequality\" title=\"Bell inequality\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwCiE\"\u003eBell inequality\u003c/a\u003e. Bell then showed that quantum physics predicts correlations that violate this inequality. Consequently, the only way that hidden variables could explain the predictions of quantum physics is if they are \"nonlocal\", which is to say that somehow the two particles are able to interact instantaneously no matter how widely they ever become separated.\u003csup about=\"#mwt898\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMermin1993_318-0\" rel=\"dc:references\" theories\"\u003eClassical unified field theories\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"mwCkE\"\u003eEncouraged by his success with general relativity, Einstein sought an even more ambitious geometrical theory that would treat gravitation and electromagnetism as aspects of a single entity. In 1950, he described his \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Unified_field_theory\" title=\"Unified field theory\" id=\"mwCkI\"\u003eunified field theory\u003c/a\u003e in a \u003ci id=\"mwCkM\"\u003e\u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Scientific_American\" title=\"Scientific American\" id=\"mwCkQ\"\u003eScientific American\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/i\u003e article titled \"On the Generalized Theory of Gravitation\".\u003csup about=\"#mwt918\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-322\" rel=\"dc:references\" typeof=\"mw:Extension/ref\" data-mw='{\"name\":\"ref\",\"attrs\":{},\"body\":{\"id\":\"mw-reference-text-cite_note-322\"}}'\u003e\u003ca href=\"./Albert_Einstein#cite_note-322\" id=\"mwCkU\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"mw-reflink-text\" id=\"mwCkY\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCkc\"\u003e[\u003c/span\u003e313\u003cspan class=\"cite-bracket\" id=\"mwCkg\"\u003e]\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e His attempt to find the most fundamental laws of nature won him praise but not success: a particularly conspicuous blemish of his model was that it did not accommodate the \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Strong_nuclear_force\" title=\"Strong nuclear force\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwCkk\"\u003estrong\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Weak_nuclear_force\" title=\"Weak nuclear force\" class=\"mw-redirect\" id=\"mwCko\"\u003eweak nuclear forces\u003c/a\u003e, neither of which was well understood until many years after his death. Although most researchers now believe that Einstein's approach to unifying physics was mistaken, his goal of a \u003ca rel=\"mw:WikiLink\" href=\"./Theory_of_everything\" title=\"Theory of everything\" id=\"mwCks\"\u003etheory of everything\u003c/a\u003e is one to which his successors still aspire.\u003csup about=\"#mwt921\" class=\"mw-ref reference\" id=\"cite_ref-323\" People of the Century|''Time'' Person of the Century]] (1999)\n}}}}\n| signature         = Albert Einstein signature 1934.svg\n| website           = {{Official URL}}\n| module            = {{Listen voice|filename=03 ALBERT EINSTEIN.ogg|name=Einstein|description=Speech for the [[United Jewish Appeal]]|recorded=11 April 1943}}\n}}\n{{Albert Einstein series}}\n'''Albert Einstein'''{{efn|{{IPAc-en|ˈ|aɪ|n|s|t|aɪ|n}};\u003cref name=\"NDxay\"/\u003e {{IPA|de|ˈalbɛʁt ˈaɪnʃtaɪn|lang|Albert Einstein german.ogg}}}} (14 March 1879{{snd}}18 April 1955) was a German-born\u003c!-- Please do not change this—see talk page and its many archives.--\u003e [[theoretical physicist]] best known for developing the [[theory of relativity]]. Einstein also made important contributions to [[Old quantum theory|quantum theory]].\u003cref name=\"frs\"/\u003e\u003cref name=\"YangHamilton2010\"/\u003e His [[mass–energy equivalence]] formula {{math|1=[[Mass–energy equivalence#Mass–velocity relationship|''E'' = ''mc''\u003csup\u003e2\u003c/sup\u003e]]}}, which arises from [[special relativity]], has been called \"the world's most famous equation\".\u003cref name=\"LnLVo\"/\u003e He received the 1921 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] for \"his services to theoretical physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the [[photoelectric effect]]\".\u003cref name=\"Nobel Prize\"/\u003e\n\nBorn as a subject to the [[Kingdom of Württemberg]], part of the [[German Empire]]\u003cref group=note name=GEcitizen/\u003e which he later renounced on 28 January 1896, just 6 weeks before he turned 17, avoiding [[Conscription in Germany|conscription into military service]].\u003cref\u003e{{Cite book |last=Fölsing |title=Albert Einstein |date= |year=1997 |pages=40}}\u003c/ref\u003e In 1895, he moved to [[Pavia]] to stay with his family which moved there an year earlier and then to Swiss canton of [[Aarau]], to attend an year of cantonal school ([[German language|German]]: ''Kantonsschule)''. In 1896, at the age of seventeen, he enrolled in the mathematics and physics teaching diploma program at the Swiss [[ETH Zurich|federal polytechnic school]] in Zurich, graduating in 1900. He acquired Swiss citizenship a year later, which he kept for the rest of his life, and afterwards secured a permanent position at the [[Swiss Patent Office]] in [[Bern]]. In 1905, he submitted a successful [[PhD]] dissertation to the [[University of Zurich]]. In 1914, he moved to Berlin to join the [[Prussian Academy of Sciences]] and the [[Humboldt University of Berlin]], becoming director of the [[Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics]] in 1917; he also became a [[Prussia]]n and consequently also German citizen again. In 1933, while Einstein was visiting the United States, [[Adolf Hitler's rise to power|Adolf Hitler came to power]] in Germany. Horrified by the [[Nazi Germany|Nazi]] persecution of his fellow Jews,\u003cref name=\"zE9Bz\"/\u003e he decided to remain in the US, and was granted American citizenship in 1940.\u003cref name=\"BoyerDubofsky2001\"/\u003e On the eve of [[World War II]], he endorsed [[Einstein–Szilard letter|a letter]] to President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] alerting him to the potential [[German nuclear weapons program]] and recommending that the US begin similar research, later carried out as the [[Manhattan Project]].\n\nIn 1905, sometimes described as his ''[[annus mirabilis]]'' (miracle year), he published [[Annus mirabilis papers|four groundbreaking papers]].{{sfnp|Galison|2000|p=377}} In them, he outlined a theory of the photoelectric effect, explained [[Brownian motion]], introduced his special theory of relativity, and demonstrated that if the special theory is correct, mass and energy are equivalent to each other. In 1915, he proposed a [[general theory of relativity]] that extended his system of mechanics to incorporate [[gravitation]]. A paper that he published the following year laid out the implications of general relativity for the modeling of the structure and evolution of the [[universe]] as a whole.\u003cref name=\"Nobel\"/\u003e\u003cref name=\"NYT-20151124\"/\u003e It introduced the [[cosmological constant]] and is further regarded as the first step in the field of modern theoretical [[cosmology]]. In 1917, Einstein wrote a paper which introduced the concepts of [[spontaneous emission]] and [[stimulated emission]], the latter of which is the core mechanism behind the [[laser]] and [[maser]], and which contained a trove of information that would be beneficial to developments in physics later on, such as [[quantum electrodynamics]] and [[quantum optics]].\u003cref\u003e{{Cite journal |last=Kleppner |first=Daniel |author-link=Daniel Kleppner |date=1 February 2005 |title=Rereading Einstein on Radiation |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/58/2/30/904451/Rereading-Einstein-on-RadiationThe-concepts-of |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=58 |issue=2 |pages=30–33 |bibcode=2005PhT....58b..30K |doi=10.1063/1.1897520 |issn=0031-9228}}\u003c/ref\u003e\n\nIn the middle part of his career, Einstein made important contributions to [[statistical mechanics]] and quantum theory. Especially notable was his work on the quantum physics of [[radiation]], in which light consists of particles, subsequently called [[photon]]s. With physicist [[Satyendra Nath Bose]], he laid the groundwork for [[Bose–Einstein statistics]]. For much of the last phase of his academic life, Einstein worked on two endeavors that ultimately proved unsuccessful. First, he advocated against quantum theory's introduction of fundamental randomness into science's picture of the world, objecting that \"God does not play dice\".\u003cref\u003e{{cite journal |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-05004-4 |title=Did Einstein really say that? |last=Robinson |first=Andrew |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |date=30 April 2018 |volume=557 |number=30 |page=30 |doi=10.1038/d41586-018-05004-4 |bibcode=2018Natur.557...30R |s2cid=14013938 |access-date=21 February 2021 |archive-date=9 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201109033021/https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-05004-4 |url-status=live |issn=0028-0836}}\u003c/ref\u003e Second, he attempted to devise a [[unified field theory]] by generalizing his geometric theory of gravitation to include [[electromagnetism]]. As a result, he became increasingly isolated from mainstream [[modern physics]]. Many [[list of things named after Albert Einstein|things are named after him]], including the element [[Einsteinium]]. In 1999, he was named [[Time (magazine)|''Time'']]'s [[Time 100: The Most Important People of the Century|Person of the Century]].\u003cref name=\"TIME\"\u003e{{cite magazine| title=Albert Einstein| magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]| last=Golden| first=Frederic| date=31 December 1999| url= https://time.com/archive/6598209/albert-einstein/}}\u003c/ref\u003e\n{{TOC-limit|3}}\n== Life and career ==\n=== Childhood, youth and education ===\n{{See also|Einstein family}}\n[[File:Albert Einstein age 3.jpg|thumb|upright|left|alt=A young boy with short hair and a round face, wearing a white collar and large bow, with vest, coat, skirt, and high boots. He is leaning against an ornate chair.|Einstein in 1882, age{{spaces}}3]]\nEinstein was born in [[Ulm]] as a subject to the [[Kingdom of Württemberg]] in the [[German Empire]]\u003cref group=note name=GEcitizen/\u003e on 14 March 1879.\u003cref name=\"Bio\" /\u003e His parents, secular [[Ashkenazi Jews]], were [[Hermann Einstein]], a salesman and engineer, and [[Pauline Koch]]. In 1880, the family moved to [[Munich]]'s borough of [[Ludwigsvorstadt-Isarvorstadt]], where Einstein's father and his uncle Jakob founded Elektrotechnische Fabrik J. Einstein \u0026 Cie, a company that manufactured electrical equipment based on [[direct current]].\u003cref name=\"Bio\"/\u003e\n\nWhen he was very young, his parents worried that he had a learning disability because he was very slow to learn to talk.\u003cref\u003e{{Cite book|last = Seelig|first = Carl|year = 1956|title = Albert Einstein: A Documentary Biography|publisher = Staples Press}}\u003c/ref\u003e When he was five and sick in bed, his father brought him a compass. This sparked his lifelong fascination with [[electromagnetism]]. He realized that \"Something deeply hidden had to be behind things.\"{{sfnp|Isaacson|2007|p= 13}}\n\nEinstein attended St. Peter's [[Catholic school|Catholic elementary school]] in Munich from the age of five. When he was eight, he was transferred to the [[Luitpold Gymnasium]], where he received advanced primary and then secondary school education.{{Sfnp|Stachel|2002|pp=[{{GBurl|id=OAsQ_hFjhrAC|p=59}} 59–61]}}\n\n{{multiple image\n | width = 145\n | image1 = Hermann einstein.jpg\n | alt1 =\n | image2 = Pauline Koch edit.jpg\n | alt2 =\n | footer = Einstein's parents, [[Hermann Einstein|Hermann]] and [[Pauline Einstein|Pauline]]\n}}\nIn 1894, Hermann and Jakob's company tendered for a contract to install electric lighting in Munich, but without success—they lacked the capital that would have been required to update their technology from direct current to the more efficient, [[alternating current]] alternative.\u003cref name=\"EQyag\"/\u003e The failure of their bid forced them to sell their Munich factory and search for new opportunities elsewhere. The Einstein family moved to [[Kingdom of Italy|Italy]], first to [[Milan]] and a few months later to [[Pavia]], where his father Hermann and his uncle [[:de:Jakob_Einstein|Jakob Einstein]] ran \"Einstein-Garrone National Electrotechnical Workshop\" ([[Italian language|Italian]]: ''Officine Elettrotecniche Nazionali Einstein-Garrone'') .\u003cref\u003e{{cite web |last1=University of Pavia |title=Einstein, Albert |url=http://musei.unipv.eu/msu/our-museums/historical-figures/albert-einstein/ |website=Museo per la Storia dell'Università di Pavia |publisher=University of Pavia |access-date=7 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230118175928/http://musei.unipv.eu/msu/our-museums/historical-figures/albert-einstein/ |archive-date=2023-01-18 |url-status=dead}}\u003c/ref\u003e Einstein, then fifteen, stayed behind in Munich in order to finish his schooling. His father wanted him to study [[electrical engineering]], but he was a fractious pupil who found the Gymnasium's regimen and teaching methods far from congenial. He later wrote that the school's policy of strict [[rote learning]] was harmful to creativity. At the end of December 1894, a letter from a doctor persuaded the Luitpold's authorities to release him from its care, and he joined his family in Pavia.{{Sfnp|Fölsing|1997|pp=30–31}} While in Italy as a teenager, he wrote an essay titled \"On the Investigation of the State of the [[Aether (classical element)|Ether]] in a Magnetic Field\".\u003cref name=Stachel2008\u003eStachel, et al (2008). Vol. 1 (1987), doc. 5.\u003c/ref\u003e\u003cref name=\"1RgTv\"/\u003e\n[[File:Casa foscolo.jpg|thumb|225x225px|Einstein family's residence from 1894-96, [[Palazzo Cornazzani]], Pavia.]]\nEinstein excelled at physics and mathematics from an early age, and soon acquired the mathematical expertise normally only found in a child several years his senior. He began teaching himself [[algebra]], [[calculus]] and [[Euclidean geometry]] when he was twelve; he made such rapid progress that he discovered an original proof of the [[Pythagorean theorem]] before his thirteenth birthday.\u003cref name=\"FVfDU\"/\u003e\u003cref\u003e{{cite book |title=The God Problem: How a Godless Cosmos Creates |edition=illustrated |first1=Howard |last1=Bloom |publisher=Prometheus Books |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-61614-552-1 |page=294 |url={{GBurl|id=xlEupJb4ojIC}} |access-date=8 August 2020 }}\u003c/ref\u003e A family tutor, [[Max Talmud]], said that only a short time after he had given the twelve year old Einstein a geometry textbook, the boy \"had worked through the whole book. He thereupon devoted himself to higher mathematics{{spaces}}... Soon the flight of his mathematical genius was so high I could not follow.\"{{sfnp|Isaacson|2007|p=17}} Einstein recorded that he had \"mastered [[integral]] and [[differential calculus]]\" while still just fourteen.{{sfnp|Isaacson|2007|p=16}} His love of algebra and geometry was so great that at twelve, he was already confident that nature could be understood as a \"mathematical structure\".{{sfnp|Isaacson|2007|pp=17-18}}\n\n[[File:Albert_Einstein_age_14.jpg|thumb|upright=.9|left|alt=Studio photo of a boy seated in a relaxed posture and wearing a suit, posed in front of a backdrop of scenery.|Einstein in 1893, age{{spaces}}14]]\n\nAt thirteen, when his range of enthusiasms had broadened to include music and philosophy,{{sfnp|Calaprice|Lipscombe|2005|p=8}} Talmud introduced Einstein to [[Kant]]'s ''[[Critique of Pure Reason]]''. Kant became his favorite philosopher; according to Talmud, \"At the time he was still a child, only thirteen years old, yet Kant's works, incomprehensible to ordinary mortals, seemed to be clear to him.\"{{sfnp|Isaacson|2007|p=17}}\n\nIn 1895, at the age of sixteen, Einstein sat the entrance examination for the [[ETH Zurich|federal polytechnic school]] (later the Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule, ETH) in [[Zurich]], Switzerland. He failed to reach the required standard in the general part of the test,\u003cref name=Stachel2008a\u003eStachel, et al (2008). Vol. 1 (1987), p. 11.\u003c/ref\u003e but performed with distinction in physics and mathematics.{{Sfnp|Fölsing|1997|pp=36–37}} On the advice of the polytechnic's principal, [[Albin Herzog]], he completed his secondary education at the [[Old Cantonal School Aarau|Argovian cantonal school]] (a [[Gymnasium (school)|gymnasium]]) in [[Aarau]], Switzerland, graduating in 1896.\u003cref name=\"b250\"\u003e{{cite journal | last=Hunziker | first=Herbert | title=Albert Einstein's Magic Mountain: An Aarau Education* | journal=Physics in Perspective | volume=17 | issue=1 | date=2015 | issn=1422-6944 | doi=10.1007/s00016-014-0153-5 | pages=55–69| bibcode=2015PhP....17...55H }} ref for: [[Old Cantonal School Aarau]]\u003c/ref\u003e While lodging in Aarau with the family of [[Jost Winteler]], he fell in love with Winteler's daughter, Marie. (His sister, [[Maja Einstein|Maja]], later married Winteler's son Paul.{{Sfnp|Highfield|Carter|1993|pp=21, 31, 56–57}})\n\n[[File:Albert Einstein's exam of maturity grades (color2).jpg|thumb|upright|alt=Einstein's matriculation certificate at the age of 17. The heading translates as \"The Education Committee of the Canton of Aargau\". His scores were German 5, French 3, Italian 5, History 6, Geography 4, Algebra 6, Geometry 6, Descriptive Geometry 6, Physics 6, Chemistry 5, Natural History 5, Art Drawing 4, Technical Drawing 4. 6 = very good, 5 = good, 4 = sufficient, 3 = insufficient, 2 = poor, 1 = very poor.|Einstein's ''[[Matura]]'' certificate from [[canton of Aargau]], 1896\u003cref group=note name=MaturaScore /\u003e]]\n\nThe ''[[Matura]]'' (graduation for the successful completion of higher secondary schooling), awarded to him in September 1896, acknowledged him to have performed well across most of the curriculum, allotting him a [[Grading systems by country#Switzerland|top grade of 6]] for history, physics, algebra, geometry, and descriptive geometry.\u003cref name=Stachel2008b\u003eStachel, et al (2008). Vol. 1 (1987), docs. 21–27.\u003c/ref\u003e At seventeen, he enrolled in the four-year mathematics and physics teaching diploma program at the federal polytechnic school. He befriended fellow student [[Marcel Grossmann]], who would help him there to get by despite his loose study habits, and later to mathematically underpin his revolutionary insights into physics. Marie Winteler, a year older than him, took up a teaching post in [[Olsberg, Aargau|Olsberg]], Switzerland.{{Sfnp|Highfield|Carter|1993|pp=21, 31, 56–57}}\n[[File:Albert Einstein's Württemberg nationality renunciation.jpg|left|thumb|266x266px|\"Petition by the merchant Hermann Einstein in Pavia for the release of his son Albert Einstein from [[Kingdom of Württemberg|Württemberg citizenship]]...\", 1896\u003cref group=note name=GEcitizen/\u003e]]\nThe five other polytechnic school freshmen following the same course as Einstein included just one woman, a twenty year old [[Serbs|Serbian]], [[Mileva Marić]]. Over the next few years, the pair spent many hours discussing their shared interests and learning about topics in physics that the polytechnic school's lectures did not cover. In his letters to Marić, Einstein confessed that exploring science with her by his side was much more enjoyable than reading a textbook in solitude. Eventually the two students became not only friends, but also lovers.\u003cref name=\"mileva\"\u003e{{Cite web|last=Gagnon|first=Pauline|date=19 December 2016|title=The Forgotten Life of Einstein's First Wife|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/guest-blog/the-forgotten-life-of-einsteins-first-wife/|access-date=17 October 2020|website=Scientific American Blog Network|archive-date=17 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201017222145/https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/guest-blog/the-forgotten-life-of-einsteins-first-wife/|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e\n\nHistorians of physics are divided on the question of the extent to which Marić contributed to the insights of Einstein's ''annus mirabilis'' publications. There is at least some evidence that he was influenced by her scientific ideas,\u003cref name=\"mileva\"/\u003e\u003cref name=\"7HA7H\"/\u003e\u003cref name=\"1zJdH\"/\u003e but there are scholars who doubt whether her impact on his thought was of any great significance at all.{{Sfnp|Pais|1994|pp=1–29}}\u003cref name=\"xKrMG\"/\u003e{{Sfnp|Stachel|2002|pp=[{{GBurl|id=OAsQ_hFjhrAC|p=49}} 49–56]}}\u003cref name=\"dUxMl\"/\u003e\n\n=== Marriages, relationships and children ===\n[[File:Albert Einstein and his wife Mileva Maric.jpg|thumb|Albert Einstein and [[Mileva Marić]] Einstein, 1912]]\nCorrespondence between Einstein and Marić, discovered and published in 1987, revealed that the couple had a daughter named [[Lieserl Einstein|Lieserl]]. She was born in early 1902 while Marić was visiting her parents in [[Novi Sad]]. When Marić returned to Switzerland the child was no longer with her. What happened to Lieserl is uncertain. In a letter written in September 1903, Einstein suggested that the girl was either given up for adoption or died of [[scarlet fever]] in infancy.\u003cref name=\"HBMes\"/\u003e{{sfnp|Calaprice|Lipscombe|2005|pp=22–23}}\n\nEinstein and Marić married in January 1903. In May 1904, their son [[Hans Albert Einstein|Hans Albert]] was born in [[Bern]], Switzerland. Their son [[Einstein family#Eduard \"Tete\" Einstein (Albert's second son)|Eduard]] was born in Zurich in July 1910. In letters that Einstein wrote to [[Marie Winteler]] in the months before Eduard's arrival, he described his love for his wife as \"misguided\" and mourned the \"missed life\" that he imagined he would have enjoyed if he had married Winteler instead: \"I think of you in heartfelt love every spare minute and am so unhappy as only a man can be.\"\u003cref name=\"MlQLY\" /\u003e\n\nIn 1912, Einstein entered into a relationship with [[Elsa Löwenthal]], who was both his first cousin on his mother's side and his second cousin on his father's.{{sfnp|Calaprice|Lipscombe|2005|p=[{{GBurl|id=5eWh2O_3OAQC|p=50}} 50]}}\u003cref name=\"dh\"\u003e{{cite book |last1=Hoffmann |first1=Dieter |title=Einstein's Berlin: In the footsteps of a genius |date=2013 |publisher=The Johns Hopkins University Press |location=Baltimore |isbn=978-1-4214-1040-1 |pages=2–9, 28}}\u003c/ref\u003e{{Sfnp|Stachel|1996|p=212}} When Marić learned of his infidelity soon after moving to Berlin with him in April 1914, she returned to Zurich, taking Hans Albert and Eduard with her.\u003cref name=\"mileva\"/\u003e Einstein and Marić were granted a divorce on 14 February 1919 on the grounds of having lived apart for five years.\u003cref\u003e{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/11/06/arts/dark-side-of-einstein-emerges-in-his-letters.html|title=Dark Side of Einstein Emerges in His Letters|first=Dinitia|last=Smith|newspaper=The New York Times|date=6 November 1996|access-date=17 August 2020|archive-date=5 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210105092333/https://www.nytimes.com/1996/11/06/arts/dark-side-of-einstein-emerges-in-his-letters.html|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e{{sfnp|Stachel|1996|p=219}} As part of the divorce settlement, Einstein agreed that if he were to win a Nobel Prize, he would give the money that he received to Marić; he won the prize two years later.\u003cref\u003e{{Cite web|title=Volume 9: The Berlin Years: Correspondence, January 1919 – April 1920 (English translation supplement) page 6|url=https://einsteinpapers.press.princeton.edu/vol9-trans/28|access-date=4 October 2021|website=einsteinpapers.press.princeton.edu|archive-date=4 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211004033245/https://einsteinpapers.press.princeton.edu/vol9-trans/28|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e\n\n[[File:Einstein_Albert_Elsa_LOC_32096u.jpg|alt=Einstein, looking relaxed and holding a pipe, stands next to a smiling, well-dressed Elsa who is wearing a fancy hat and fur wrap. She is looking at him.|left|thumb|Albert and [[Elsa Einstein]] arriving in New York, 1921]]\nEinstein married Löwenthal in 1919.{{sfnp|Isaacson|2007|p=xix}}{{Sfnp|Calaprice|Kennefick|Schulmann|2015|p=62}} In 1923, he began a relationship with a secretary named Betty Neumann, the niece of his close friend Hans Mühsam.\u003cref\u003e{{Cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/northamerica/usa/1523626/Einsteins-theory-of-fidelity.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220110/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/northamerica/usa/1523626/Einsteins-theory-of-fidelity.html |archive-date=10 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Einstein's theory of fidelity|first=Roger|last=Highfield|date=10 July 2006|work=The Daily Telegraph}}{{cbignore}}\u003c/ref\u003e\u003cref\u003e{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/04/17/science/albert-einstein-genius-national-geographic-channel.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170418100011/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/04/17/science/albert-einstein-genius-national-geographic-channel.html |archive-date=18 April 2017 |url-access=limited |title='Genius' Unravels the Mysteries of Einstein's Universe| first=Dennis| last=Overbye| newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=17 April 2017}}\u003c/ref\u003e\u003cref\u003e{{Cite web|url=https://www.natgeotv.com/za/special/genius-albert-einsteins-theory-of-infidelity|title=Genius Albert Einstein's Theory of Infidelity|publisher=NatGeo TV|access-date=9 August 2020|archive-date=23 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200923010851/https://www.natgeotv.com/za/special/genius-albert-einsteins-theory-of-infidelity|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e\u003cref\u003e{{Cite news|url=https://www.jpost.com/health-and-science/getting-up-close-and-personal-with-einstein|title=Getting up close and personal with Einstein|website=The Jerusalem Post \u0026#124; JPost.com|access-date=29 August 2020|archive-date=23 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200923001654/https://www.jpost.com/Health-and-Science/Getting-up-close-and-personal-with-Einstein|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e Löwenthal nevertheless remained loyal to him, accompanying him when he emigrated to the United States in 1933. In 1935, she was diagnosed with heart and kidney problems. She died in December 1936.{{Sfnp|Highfield|Carter|1993|p=216}}\n\nA volume of Einstein's letters released by the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] in 2006\u003cref\u003e{{Cite web|url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/india/einstein-secret-love-affairs-out/story-QVSHrfMYJzCRcIlbBCJKAM.html|title=Einstein secret love affairs out!|date=13 July 2006|website=Hindustan Times|access-date=17 August 2020|archive-date=23 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200923115250/https://www.hindustantimes.com/india/einstein-secret-love-affairs-out/story-QVSHrfMYJzCRcIlbBCJKAM.html|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e added some other women with whom he was romantically involved. They included Margarete Lebach (a married Austrian),\u003cref\u003e{{Cite book |last=Graydon |first=Samuel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PRSsEAAAQBAJ\u0026dq=Margarete+Lebach\u0026pg=PA199 |title=Einstein in Time and Space: A Life in 99 Particles |date=14 November 2023 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-1-9821-8512-1 |edition=1 |location=New York |pages=199 |language=en}}\u003c/ref\u003e Estella Katzenellenbogen (the rich owner of a florist business), Toni Mendel (a wealthy Jewish widow) and Ethel Michanowski (a Berlin socialite), with whom he spent time and from whom he accepted gifts while married to Löwenthal.\u003cref\u003e{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna13804030|title=New letters shed light on Einstein's love life|date=11 July 2006|publisher=NBC News|access-date=15 August 2020|archive-date=22 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200222022647/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/13804030/ns/technology_and_science-science/t/new-letters-shed-light-einsteins-love-life|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e\u003cref\u003e{{Cite news|url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/magazines/panache/albert-einstein-may-have-had-the-iq-but-he-needed-to-work-on-his-eq/articleshow/64849211.cms?from=mdr|title=Albert Einstein may have had the IQ, but he needed to work on his EQ|newspaper=The Economic Times|access-date=15 August 2020|archive-date=8 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210208134808/https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/magazines/panache/albert-einstein-may-have-had-the-iq-but-he-needed-to-work-on-his-eq/articleshow/64849211.cms?from=mdr|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e After being widowed, Einstein was briefly in a relationship with {{ill|Margarita Konenkova|ru|Конёнкова, Маргарита Ивановна}}, thought by some to be a Russian spy;{{refn|group=note|The claim that Konenkova was a spy is based on [[Special Tasks]], a discredited memoir by [[Pavel Sudoplatov]].\u003cref\u003e{{Cite web |last=Levy |first=Josh |date=30 November 2023 |title=Love and Intrigue at Princeton: Newly Opened Letters from Einstein's Love Affair with Margarita Konenkova {{!}} Unfolding History |url=https://blogs.loc.gov/manuscripts/2023/11/love-and-intrigue-at-princeton-newly-opened-letters-from-einsteins-love-affair-with-margarita-konenkova |access-date=21 July 2026 |website=The Library of Congress}}\u003c/ref\u003e}} her husband, the Russian sculptor [[Sergei Konenkov]], created the bronze bust of Einstein at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] at Princeton.\u003cref\u003e{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/06/01/us/love-letters-by-einstein-at-auction.html|title=Love Letters By Einstein at Auction|first=Robin|last=Pogrebin|newspaper=The New York Times|date=1 June 1998|access-date=10 August 2020|archive-date=7 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201107053956/https://www.nytimes.com/1998/06/01/us/love-letters-by-einstein-at-auction.html|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e\u003cref\u003e{{Cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/einsteins-letters-show-affair-with-spy-1162418.html|title=Einstein's letters show affair with spy|date=2 June 1998|website=The Independent|access-date=10 November 2020|archive-date=16 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201116013010/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/einsteins-letters-show-affair-with-spy-1162418.html|url-status=live}}\u003c/ref\u003e\n\nFollowing an episode of acute mental illness at about the age of twenty, Einstein's son Eduard was diagnosed with [[schizophrenia]].\u003cref name=\"Robinson2015a\"/\u003e He spent the remainder of his life either in the care of his mother or in temporary confinement in an asylum.
